title: From School Dropout to IPO: How Sathish Kumar Built the Rs 10,000 Crore Milky Mist Dairy Empire
excerpt: The Erode teenager who taught himself to make paneer is now taking his dairy company public with a Rs 1,553 crore offering
body:
• T. Sathish Kumar dropped out of school as a teenager in Erode, Tamil Nadu, to revive his family's struggling milk business, teaching himself to make paneer through months of trial and error.
  • Milky Mist has grown from a 10 kg batch of paneer sold in Bengaluru in 1993 to Rs 3,145 crore in revenue for FY26, with over 350 SKUs across 20-plus product categories.
  • The company launched its Rs 1,553 crore IPO on August 11, 2026, at a price band of Rs 133-140 per share and an expected valuation of Rs 10,310-10,778 crore.
  • Milky Mist processes nearly one million litres of milk daily from 70,000 farmers and claims roughly 60 percent market share in paneer across South India.

In the early 1990s, a teenager named Sathish Kumar T. was riding in a milk truck between Erode, Tamil Nadu, and Bengaluru, helping his family's modest dairy trading operation survive. Thirty-five years later, he is the chairman and managing director of Milky Mist Dairy Food Limited, a company valued at over Rs 10,000 crore that just launched its initial public offering.

A Teenager Bets on Paneer

Kumar's family originally ran a power loom business in Erode that eventually shut down. They pivoted to milk trading, procuring and transporting around 3,000 litres daily to Bengaluru. The business struggled — Kumar's uncle exited in 1990, and the operation closed in 1992.

At around 15, Kumar left school to salvage what remained. He noticed a Bengaluru customer converting milk into paneer for hotels. Paneer had almost no presence in South Indian households at the time — as The Hindu BusinessLine noted, in Tamil Nadu, "paneer" still meant paneer soda, a rose water drink.

With no training and no internet, Kumar spent months experimenting — heating milk and using vinegar to curdle it until the texture was right. In 1993, he carried his first 10 kg batch to Bengaluru. By 1995, Milky Mist was moving 50 to 100 kg daily.

"No Google or YouTube videos those days to learn. I will talk to paneer and milk."

— T. Sathish Kumar, CMD, Milky Mist Dairy Food

Building a Brand by Accident

Kumar never planned to build a brand. In 1997, when a Foodworld supermarket purchase manager asked for a brand name, Kumar did not know what branding meant. He went to a browsing centre, searched Yahoo, and picked "Milky Mist" from a shortlist.

Rather than selling liquid milk — perishable and thin-margin — he redirected all procurement toward value-added products. In 2005, Milky Mist exited liquid milk entirely. The product range expanded to curd, butter, cheese, yoghurt, ice cream, and chocolates under the Capella sub-brand. The company also acquired Asal, a ready-to-cook brand. Today, it produces over 350 SKUs across more than 20 categories.

Automation and the Cold Chain Bet

A 2009 visit to a dairy trade fair in Hanover was a turning point. Kumar invested in a fully automated plant at Perundurai, spread over 55 acres, replacing the original two-acre facility. It now processes close to one million litres of milk per day from approximately 70,000 farmers across 12 Tamil Nadu districts.

In 2018, Milky Mist installed a robotic paneer and curd processing line; an automated cheese plant followed in 2019. The facility runs on 100 percent green energy — 14 MW solar and 2 MW wind.

Kumar also built the entire cold chain in-house. Milky Mist operates 280 refrigerated trucks across the country. CEO K. Rathnam, a former managing director of Amul Dairy, told The Hindu BusinessLine that outsourcing logistics had burned them — drivers would switch off truck refrigeration and turn it back on at delivery time.

"This is farm to fork, everything is in our hand."

— T. Sathish Kumar, CMD, Milky Mist Dairy Food

Where Milky Mist Stands Today

Revenue stood at Rs 42 crore in 2012. By FY24 it reached Rs 1,826 crore, climbing to Rs 2,354 crore in FY25 and Rs 3,145 crore in FY26. Profit after tax rose from Rs 19.44 crore in FY24 to Rs 127 crore in FY26. The company claims roughly 60 percent market share in branded paneer across South India, with products now available nationwide.

Kumar's office remains above the factory floor — a 12-minute commute from his home. Asked about competition at a recent Bengaluru industry event, he offered an unexpected answer: "Meat and chicken are my competitors," pointing to the broader protein consumption opportunity.

The IPO and What Comes Next

Milky Mist launched its Rs 1,553 crore IPO on August 11, 2026, comprising a fresh issue of Rs 1,428 crore and an offer-for-sale of Rs 125 crore. The price band is Rs 133-140 per share, implying a valuation of approximately Rs 10,310-10,778 crore. The issue closes on August 13.

Ahead of the offering, the company raised Rs 465.30 crore from anchor investors by allocating 3.32 crore equity shares at Rs 140 each. Kumar has consistently resisted private equity, telling The Hindu BusinessLine that PE investors' perception differs from his as an entrepreneur. The company funded growth primarily through bank debt — at one point borrowing Rs 480 crore when revenue was only Rs 200 crore.

From a teenager experimenting with vinegar and milk in a small Tamil Nadu town to a company commanding a potential Rs 10,000 crore-plus valuation, Kumar's trajectory is one of the more striking entrepreneurship stories in India's food industry.
nri_angle: Milky Mist's IPO and national expansion highlight how a small-town Indian dairy brand built on paneer — a staple in diaspora kitchens worldwide — is entering public markets.
author: Diaspora Desk
